label: section_header
text: Executive summary

label: text
text: This report, commissioned by IP Australia and conducted by the Centre for Transformative Innovation at Swinburne University of Technology, investigates the alignment of the scope of patent triplets: those granted by IP Australia a those granted by the European Patent Office (EPO) and the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).

label: text
text: The study focuses on the impact of the Raising the Bar (RTB) reforms introduced in Australia in 2013 and aimed at narrowing the scope of Australian patents to align with international standards. A comprehensive methodology was employed, including a manual assessment of 500 patent triplets and the development of a supervised Machine Learning (ML) model to predict patent scope across a larger sample of over 80,000 patent triplets. This innovative approach leveraged labeled data from manual assessments and ML predictions for empirical analysis.

label: section_header
text: Key findings:

label: list_item
text: The RTB reforms significantly aligned Australian patent claims with international standards, potentially reducing the probability of Australian patents being broader than their international counterparts by up to 5 percentage points.

label: list_item
text: Despite the reforms, approximately a third of Australian patents examined after the reforms have claims that appear to be broader than their international equivalents.

label: list_item
text: The impact of the reforms was most pronounced in patents within the CHEM and ELEC examination sections of IP Australia, most likely reflecting differential impacts across different technological areas.

label: text
text: The report suggests that while the RTB reforms have been effective in narrowing the scope of Australian patents towards international norms, there remains room for further aligning IP Australia patent examination outcomes to those of the EPO and/or the USPTO. The study also demonstrates the potential value from leveraging new AI and ML tools for patent classification and scope assessment in combination with expert input from patent examiners, paving the way for more informed policy decisions and patent quality improvements.

label: section_header
text: Introduction 1

label: text
text: A patent is a temporary exclusive right to exclude others from exploiting (making, using or selling) an invention protected by the patent. The boundary of the patent owner's right to exclude is defined by the patent claims, which describe the key inventive features of the patentee's idea. The scope of the granted patent claims may be broad (an incandescent lamp) or narrow (an incandescent lamp using a carbonised bamboo filament). It ultimately determines the number of competing products and processes that could be deemed as infringing the patent (Merges and Nelson, 1990). Therefore, the scope of the granted patent claims influences the patent's value and its impact on investment and competition.

label: text
text: IP Australia commissioned the Centre for Transformative Innovation at Swinburne University of Technology (CTI) to assess whether the scope of the claims of patents granted in Australia aligns with the scope of the claims of equivalent patents (the set of "identical" patents which belong to the same patent family) granted by the European Patent Office (EPO) and the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO). 1 The objective of the analysis is to understand how the relative scope of patents granted in Australia has changed over time and evaluate the impact of Australia's Raising the Bar (RTB) reforms, which came into effect in 2013 and were intended in part to narrow the scope of patents granted in Australia to align with other major jurisdictions. This report details the design and findings of the study.

label: text
text: The research consists of 2 stages. The first stage is based on a small sample of triplet (that is, IP Australia-EPO-USPTO) patents. Specifically, to evaluate the scope of patent claims, we tasked a team of patent examiners at IP Australia with manually assessing a random sample of 500 "patent triplets" - collections of patent application families covering the same or similar technical content which were granted by IP Australia, the EPO and the USPTO - for their relative patent scope.

label: text
text: We assess relative patent scope as the scope of an Australian patent compared to the scope of its equivalent patent granted in Europe and, separately, to the scope of its equivalent patent granted in the United States.

label: text
text: The second stage aims to scale up the claim scope comparison beyond the original 500 sample by leveraging machine learning and natural language processing techniques to reduce the amount of research time and funding required. 2 In this stage, we used the labelled data from the manual assessment of 500 randomly selected patent triplets of the first stage to develop a supervised Machine Learning (ML) model for predicting the relative scope for a large sample of patent triplets. 3 Thus, in essence, the second stage automates the claim scope comparison of the first stage. The sample of second stage covers virtually the whole population of patent triplets granted by IP Australia, the EPO and USPTO with examination request years between 2000 and 2019. After ensuring that there is complete information on the claim text of the patents, we end up with over 80,000 patent triplets. In the second stage we used both the manually assessed sample and the ML model predictions for the empirical analysis to assess the impact of the Raising the Bar reform.

label: text
text: Overall, we find strong evidence that the Raising the Bar Reforms were an effective tool to align Australian patent claims with international standards. In particular, the reforms may have resulted in up to a 5 percentage point reduction in the probability of Australian patents being broader than their international equivalent in either the United States or the European Union. As we found evidence that prior to the reform that up to 40% of Australian patents were broader than their corresponding patent, the result indicates both a substantial improvement, but also suggests further reforms may be required if Australia desires to align granted patent scope to the United States and European Union.

label: section_header
text: Patent scope: A key patent setting 2

label: section_header
text: Patent systems and patent scope

label: text
text: The patent system is a fundamental pillar for supporting industrial advancement and the growth of knowledge, which in turn fuels longterm economic growth. However, it can also limit the freedom to operate and enforce licensing fees for the use of patented knowledge, essentially allowing patent holders to set prices for the use of their inventions. This can discourage innovation by making it more expensive and difficult to diffuse the patented knowledge. To mitigate these negative effects and encourage innovation and its widespread adoption, the patent system requires that an invention be new, non-obvious, and useful before it can be patented. Without such criteria, patents could be misused to block competing technologies excessively, thereby impeding industrial progress and development.

label: text
text: In addition, the patent system can also limit the scope of the rights granted to the patent owner to exclude others from exploiting the patented invention. Patent scope refers to the degree or breadth of exclusive rights that a patent confers and corresponds to the generality of the patent's claims. Alongside the duration of the property right, a patent's scope helps determine its economic significance; "the broader the scope, the larger the number of competing products and processes that will infringe the patent" (Merges and Nelson, 1990). As a large literature shows, patent scope has an important influence on patent value, patent litigation, investment and patent strategy (Marco et al., 2019).

label: caption
text: Figure 1: Breadth of patents.

label: text
text: For illustration on patent scope, Knight (2013) conceptualised the breadth of the scope of patent protection using fencing as an analogy, as shown in Figure 1. Patent holders may try to obtain a relatively broad patent to cover a large domain of knowledge (Figure 1a) or a large number of narrow patents covering that domain (Figure 1b). While there may be value in seeking broad patents, firms may find in practice that the fence has holes that competitors can use to their advantage (Figure 1c).

label: text
text: Patent scope is essential to conversations in legal and public policy domains regarding patent quality and the optimal patent settings from an economic perspective. The scope of patents is a significant concern as granting patent rights for overly broad or vague claims can impose deadweight losses - costs to society created by market inefficiency and inefficient allocation of resources (Abramowicz and Duffy, 2011). Policy makers have sought to influence the scope of granted patents as an important lever to influence patent value, incentives for innovation, and the welfare consequences from deadweight loss (Gilbert and Shapiro, 1990; Klemperer, 1990).

label: section_header
text: Measuring patent scope

label: text
text: Unlike patent duration, which can be measured in years and regulated by establishing a maximum term for protection and by charging renewal fees, patent scope is harder to measure. Researchers have experimented with a variety of methods for analysing patent scope and applied these to assess the impacts of patent policy and examination practice. Two early strategies included counting the number of claims in the patent (Lanjouw and Schankerman, 1997) or counting the number of technological classifications assigned to the patent by the examination authority (Lerner, 1994). However, it is not clear how reliable these approaches are. For example, until recently, proponents of the former approach have tended not to differentiate between independent and dependent claims. The breadth of the intellectual property covered by a patent is represented by a set of claims. Most claims in a typical patent are "dependent" claims which reference and qualify independent claims (Harhoff, 2016). A patent's legal right to exclude is defined by its independent claims, which do not refer to any other claim in the patent application and are the broadest of claims.

label: text
text: More recent studies have attempted to measure patent scope as the number of independent claims in a patent grant (Marco et al., 2019). However, Kuhn and Thompson (2019) found the independent claim count to be "uninformative" of patent scope. Other scholars have proposed using the word count of a patent's first (independent) claim as a proxy measure for scope, with more words corresponding to narrower scope. The logic behind this approach is that patent claims that include more words are likely to contain more conditioning statements that narrow the scope of the intellectual property. Kuhn and Thompson (2019) found strong agreement between scope measurement based on patent claim length and attorneys' assessments of scope for a sample of patents. Other recent work has attempted to evaluate patent scope using semantic analysis of the claim text. For example, Wittfoth (2019) focuses on regular expressions to detect language typically used to determine if a claim within the patent is dependent or independent of the first claim. The output is fed into an algorithm that calculates an estimate for patent scope.

label: section_header
text: The RTB reforms' objectives

label: text
text: While there is no international agreement which seeks to define or harmonise patent scope, all patent systems employ legal doctrines to regulate patent scope. For example, one such doctrine is the adequacy of the written description, or scope of embodiments (inventions that embody a given idea) encompassed by claim language for infringement. At the heart of the patent system is a bargain: in exchange for the right to exclude, an applicant must disclose new technical knowledge in their invention. The disclosure must be sufficient to enable a person having ordinary skill in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. The scope of claims over which patent rights are granted is closely tied to the amount of technical information that the applicant discloses to support enablement within the patent application; enablement places "an outer limit on the scope of the claims" (Seymore, 2008).

label: text
text: The IP Laws Amendment (Raising the Bar) Act 2012 was a substantial overhaul of the IP system within Australia and intended to support innovation across several key areas. In particular, the reforms intended to raise the quality of granted patents to better align with international standards (IP Australia, 2013). The reforms, which took effect in April 2013, were intended to affect several areas of patent scope as well as the patent examination process. Owens (2013) notes several aspects of the reforms relevant to our study in this report:

label: list_item
text: Patent specifications must demonstrate a "specific, substantial and credible use" for the invention

label: list_item
text: Patent specifications must allow someone familiar with the subject matter to be able to reproduce the invention

label: list_item
text: The inventive step must be compared to general knowledge globally, not just within Australia

label: list_item
text: Patent examiners are able to consider and report on the usefulness and prior use in their examination.

label: text
text: To assess whether the Raising the Bar reform resulted in a change in scope to align with international standards, we develop a method that tests for meaningful differences in equivalent patent applications (i.e., patents for the same or similar inventions granted in different international jurisdictions) (Palangkaraya et al., 2011; Christie et al., 2016). Measuring the relative scope of patents granted in Australia allows us to assess how the scope of patents granted in Australia changed before and after the RTB reforms, relative to patents granted overseas.

label: section_header
text: A manual and a machine learning approaches to measure relative patent scope

label: section_header
text: Manual assessment of relative patent scope

label: text
text: For the first stage of the study, we draw a random sample of patent triplets containing one patent granted at IP Australia, one patent granted at the EPO, and one patent granted at the USPTO, all of which has an identical patent family ID, using bulk patent data from these IP offices. The population from which the sample was drawn contains 80,199 families of patent triplets. This population represents largely the entire population of such triplets with one important restriction: that there is only a unique patent family member within each jurisdiction. The population is also limited only to those patent families from which the corresponding Australian patent family member had undergone an examination request from 2000 through to 2019.

label: text
text: More specifically, the study contains eligible granted patent families, where each granted patent (identified by their DOCDB patent family identifier) had the following characteristics:

label: list_item
text: Corresponding application numbers f ound within the EPO, IP Australia and USPTO databases

label: list_item
text: Cannot have more than one corresponding patent within the patent family for any of the focal jurisdictions

label: list_item
text: Application kind "B" is a granted patent

label: list_item
text: Examination request date between 2000 and 2019 (inclusive).

label: section_header

label: text
text: We then randomly draw 500 granted triplet patent families from the subset where the Australian examination request date was between 2010 and 2016. 4 These patent families were apportioned equally, from the following IP Australiaexamination sections: CHEM2, CHEM3, ELEC1, ELEC2 and MECH2. Patent examiners employed at IP Australia then applied their expertise in the aforementioned examination sections to manually assess the patent triplets for their relative scope. That is, for each patent granted by IP Australia in the sample of 500, they compared the scope of the granted patent claims to the scope of the equivalent granted patent claims granted by the EPO or, separately, by the USPTO.

label: text
text: Using a five-point Likert scale, as shown in Figure 2, examiners at IP Australia were asked to assess for each Australian granted patent the relative scope of its first claim against that in the EPO equivalent and separately against the USPTO equivalent. The examiners were further asked to evaluate the relative scope based on all claims in each patent. The question for a given patent would read similar to:

label: text
text: "The scope of the Australian claim compared to the USPTO (EPO) claim is ..."

label: text
text: to which they are expected to choose one of the points in the Likert scale.

label: text
text: In their manual assessment, the examiners were asked to compare patent pairs for their relative scope based on both the first claim set (the first independent claims in the Australian patent and its overseas equivalent) and the set of all claims (the full set of claims in the patent pairs). The manual assessment based on both claim sets allows for testing whether the first claim is a good predictor of the scope of all claims within a granted patent.

label: text
text: Figure 3 charts the distribution of relative patent scope for the first claim (left panel) and for all claims (right panel), showing how the distribution changed before and after the RTB reforms. The figures show a similar distribution across the set of first and all claims. Before the reforms, nearly half of Australian patent claims were assessed to be relatively similar to the claims in their overseas equivalents. A minority share of Australian patents were assessed to be broader than their overseas equivalents, while a smaller minority were assessed to be narrower.

label: section_header
text: Evaluating relative patent scope using machine learning models

label: text
text: We use the manually assessed relative scope of Australian patents discussed above within a selection of supervised machine learning algorithms to predict the relative scope for the full set of Australian patents with equivalent patents granted at the USPTO and EPO. The objective is to leverage the labeled data and the ML predictive models to scale up the analysis of relative patent scope across the three patent offices and the impact of the RTB reform beyond the relatively small 500 manual assessment sample.

label: text
text: Similar to a traditional econometric approach, where we would model the relationship of an outcome variable as a function of several explanatory variables, a supervised machine learning (ML) classifier algorithm uses several "features" to classify the relative patent scope for each patent pair. The predictive features in the ML modelling were generated based on bibliometric characteristics of the patents including:

label: list_item
text: Year of exam request,

label: list_item
text: 4-digit International Patent Classification (IPC) codes for a patent's technology area,

label: list_item
text: IP Australia's examination section, and

label: list_item
text: Country of origin.

label: text
text: Most importantly, we also generated predictive features on textual characteristics of the claims (the first claim and all claim sets). 6 These include:

label: list_item
text: The relative word count difference between the Australian patent and its international pair, and

label: list_item
text: Various measures of semantic and syntactic similarity.

label: text
text: The complete list of features and details on the modeling approach is provided in Appendix B.

label: text
text: We assess the quality of the modelling by testing the model parameters using data that was not used to train the model.

label: text
text: To select the best machine learning model, we use the F1 score (described in detail within Appendix B) as the ranking criterion. The intent was to find the best balance between precision and recall - i.e., between excluding false negatives and excluding false positives from our predicted classifications. Extensive methodological work was also undertaken in visual analysis and outlier detection, and in hyperparameter tuning and crossvalidation. Based on this ML modelling strategy, the Multilayer perceptron classifier (MLP Classifier) was subsequently selected to generate the data for the main descriptive and regression analyses due to the F1 scores for both the set of first claims and the set of all claims within a patent.

The figure shows a spike in examination requests in 2013, when the Raising the Bar reforms came into effect. A detailed analysis of Australian patent data concluded that most examination requests in 2013 occurred prior to the starting date of the reforms. This suggests that applicants may have believed that the reforms were likely to have an impact on the scope of their patents if they did not request examination before the deadline.

A closer look reveals that the decreasing trends appear to start in 2010, three years prior to the RTB reform. Therefore, consistent with our discussion of Figure 7, RTB reforms appear to be associated with a decrease in the proportion of broader patents from 2013 to 2015. However, since the downward trend began in 2010, it is plausible that a portion of the effects of RTB reforms might have been anticipated. 11

label: text
text: Furthermore, Figure 8 also highlights the discrepancy in the trend exhibited by AU-EP and AU-US comparisons, especially prior to 2010, where the proportion of AU patents classified as broader compared to US patents is as much as 10 percentage points (or around 30%) higher than compared to EP patents and also that AU patents were increasingly more likely to be broader than US patents between 2005 and 2010. It is not clear what caused the significant discrepancy in those years, however, the average word count differences shown in Figure 7 earlier do suggest that AU patent claims (first or all claims) tend to be shorter compared to US patent claims and longer compared to EP patent claims. We should also note that the changes in the relative scope may also reflect any change implemented in the European and American patent systems.

label: text
text: It is also interesting to note that the proportion of broader AU patents appears to be slightly on the rise again post-2015. However, the rate of increase appears to be relatively negligible. For example, looking at AU-EP first claim plot in the red colour, the proportion of broader AU patents increased from around 0.32 in 2015 to around 0.34 in 2019 (a two percentage points or around 6% increase). It is plausible that this increase is not a statistically significant increase when we consider the 95% confidence interval of the ML Classifier prediction.

text: Quantitative estimates of the impact of RTB reforms 5

label: section_header
text: Empirical framework

label: text
text: The primary goal of the RTB reforms was to align the Australian patent system more closely with international practice. In principle, a better alignment would mean the scope of Australian patents are less likely to be broader than the scope of patents within the same family granted by other jurisdictions. Prior to the RTB reforms, the general consensus was that Australian patent claims were likely to be broader (instead of narrower) than their international counterparts (Owens, 2013). This is also confirmed by our descriptive visual analysis in the preceding chapter. The focus of the empirical analysis discussed below is to provide evidence for whether the reforms were effective in lowering the distribution of patent claims deemed to be broader.

label: text
text: Therefore, without loss of generality, to formally test and quantify the impact of the RTB reforms, we state the following testable hypothesis: 13

label: section_header
text: RTB reforms decrease the likelihood that the scope of Australian patent claims is broader than the corresponding international counterparts?

label: text
text: We test the hypothesis by estimating a linear probability regression model where the dependent variable is a binary variable with a value of 1 if the patent scope is Broader and 0 if the patent scope is Not Broader: 14

label: text
text: where i indexes each pair AU-EP and AU-US patents in the estimating sample, Scopei is the manually assessed or ML classified relative scope based on the first (or all) claims, RTBi is an indicator with a value of 1 if the corresponding Australian patent has an exam request date after the RTB reforms date (16 April 2013) and 0 otherwise, and is a set of explanatory variables including an indicator variable if the patent pair is AU-US, common text similarity measures, and indicator variables for the exam sections. Lastly, represent an unobserved error term assumed to be random.

label: text
text: To interpret the key parameter of interest , we note that while the model is a linear probability model estimated using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), it is functionally equivalent to a Difference-in-Differences model with the first difference represented by the AU-EP and AU-US claim comparisons. Therefore, we interpret as the impact of the RTB reforms on the change in patent scope in Australia. 15 This interpretation should generally hold insofar as there were no other relevant policy changes either within Australia, the European Union (EU) or US.

label: text
text: The following sections present and discuss the estimation results of the empirical model specified in equation (1) above using different sets of estimating sample and control variables. First, for the baseline estimates, we use the 500 patent triplets in which the relative scope of Australian patents was manually assessed by patent examiners. However, due to its limited sample size, the baseline estimates may not have enough statistical power to test our main hypothesis. Therefore, as our main analysis, we focus the estimation of equation (1) using the full set of 85,879 patent triplets based on the predictions of our ML Classifier models.

label: section_header
text: Discussion 6

label: text
text: Overall, we found significant (statistically and in magnitude) evidence that the Raising the Bar (RTB) reforms were an effective tool to better align Australian patent claims with the international standards. First, the impact of Raising the Bar reforms could reach as high as 5.7 percentage point reduction in the probability of Australian patent having a broader scope. This is not a trivial effect in relative terms, given that on average 40% of Australian patents in the triplet family data are considered as broader. The results from the regression model estimates using different subsamples of the data showed around 30% reduction in the proportion of Australian patent claims classified as broader than the corresponding European and American patent claims. However, this still leaves us with roughly a third of Australian patents which appear to be broader than their international counterparts.

label: text
text: When exploring the effectiveness of the reforms by examination section, we found evidence that the effects were most prominent for patents within the CHEM examination sections. However, further examination suggested that the differential impacts across the sections were likely to be related to the underlying technological area of the patents. We, found, for example, electrical patents which are under the ELEC examination section with a stronger RTB impact compared to any technology area under the CHEM examination section.

label: text
text: Furthermore, we found the impact estimates to be robust in terms of a number of factors such as how the sample window was defined and the exam section handling the patent examination. Lastly, we found that the decrease in the proportion of broader patents corresponded with a slight increase in the proportion of narrower patents and a larger increase in the proportion of similar patents. In other words, it appears the RTB reforms led to Australian patents becoming more similar to their EP and US equivalents.

label: text
text: The analysis also revealed that some of the effects of the RTB reforms could have been anticipated or that there are other factors (which may or may not be related to the RTB reform) which, starting around 2010, led to a decline in the proportion of broader AU patents. If these unknown factors were related to the RTB reforms, then the full impact of the RTB reforms would be higher than indicated by the estimates presented in the report. However, if these factors were unrelated to the RTB reforms, then some components of the estimated impacts of RTB may not be attributable to the reforms.

label: text
text: Lastly, from a methodological perspective, this report demonstrates new possibilities in how supervised Machine Learning (ML) methods combined with human expert inputs can be used to improve the quality of assessing patent scope for a large scale policy impact analysis. In fact, there is evidence that relying on previous methods of assessing patent scope such as claim word count may ultimately result in poor accuracy. The implications of poor accuracy can have real consequences as our conclusions would be largely inconclusive.

label: text
text: To enable a highly disaggregated estimation of the RTB reforms' impacts requires a much larger sample size than the original manual validation sample data. For the future, increasing the size of the manually validated sample could turn out to be highly valuable for improving econometric analysis of the reforms. Given that our sample of manually assessed patents did not cover the full spectrum of examination sections within IP Australia, further work may be needed to confirm how the reforms influenced the scope of patents outside of our sample.

label: text
text: Fortunately, the labelled data provided by the manual validation exercise did enable the development of relatively accurate supervised Machine Learning (ML) models to predict relative patent scope for virtually all of the AU-EP-US patent triplet families for which data are available. A crucial step was undertaken to extend and refine the ML models along various dimensions in the implementation of extensive cross-validation and the use of F1-score to arrive at the best machine learning models. In addition, the ML models add a long list of predictive features including extensive incorporation of International Patent Classification (IPC) codes associated with each patent family and extensive hyperparameter tuning.

label: text
text: As noted earlier, the model predictions were driven largely by the various text similarity measures and were not heavily reliant on the International Patent Classification (IPC) codes for accurate predictions. Further exploration could be conducted to better understand whether more nuanced classifications such as incorporating the full suite of classifications or using ML methods to classify the technological scope of patents may yield useful information to improve the accuracy of the patent scope modelling.

label: section_header
text: European Patent Office

label: text
text: European Patent Office (EPO) data was delivered in Extensible Markup Language (XML) format. XML format allows data to be stored in the form of the string, where symbols allow the reader to annotate parts of the string (sub-strings) as belonging to a certain category. Essentially, XMLs are databases expressed as strings, meaning that all bibliometric and text information related to a patent application will be contained in the string. The inevitable drawback being that a machine must iterate over the entirety of the string to extract relevant information, i.e., completeness at the cost of speed/ ease of handling data. As a result, we were able to cleanly pull all relevant EPO patent claims.

label: section_header
text: United States Patent Office

label: text
text: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) data is stored as multiple databases (USPTO, 2023). The databases are organised by patent aspects, for example, patent claims are stored within their own database. Although this allows us to read in the relevant database, database management can result in data loss or corruption and the databases can only be merged with another using a unique identifier. The data is stored as Tab-Separated Values (TSV) format.

label: section_header
text: IP Australia

label: text
text: IP Australia's archives are presently available as PDF files. PDFs have varying compatibility, de- pending on the year that they were created in and that was used. This means PDFs are not always convertible to TSV or Comma-Separated Values (CSV) format (formats required for machine learning). This process becomes more complicated when the patent claim text contains formulae.

label: text
text: Given that claims data was not easily machine readable via the IP Australia database, we scraped the Australian patent claim data from the public Google patent website (Alphabet, 2023). The process was carried out using the Python package Beautiful Soup. The process was far from ideal and results in claims text breaking down, instances where the text gets converted to non-English or non-sensical words, formulae and chemical structures break down into meaningless symbols and on occasion the text pulled belongs to a different patent application. The data then required further cleaning and management which is described in the later sections of the Appendix.

label: text
text: Another option that became available was to utilise an Application Programming Interface (API) via IP Australia to access the claims text. This was a particularly attractive option as we were able to utilise an official channel for obtaining patent claims text that would be less subject to changes rather than relying either on Optical Character Recognition (OCR) software on the PDF documents or scraping text from a website. Using a software package called Postman, we generated a short Python script to access the Australian Patent Search API. We then tested the output for a couple of example patents and compared the text to the pre-existing data we had scraped. One particular example was patent #2002235407 which is a patent for a Bone Screw which can be found in Figure 12.

text: Appendix D - Assessing the pre-RTB Downtrend

label: text
text: As shown in Figure 8 and mentioned in the discussion of the baseline regression estimates presented in Tables 1 and 2, the proportion of broader patents has been in a downward trend prior to the RTB reforms. This pre-reform downward trend could be caused by an anticipatory factor related to the RTB reforms or an unknown factor unrelated to the reforms. If the former, then the estimated impact shown in Tables 1 and 2 may be biased downward. In contrast, if the driving cause of the pre-reform downtrend is unrelated to the reforms, then the impact of the reforms has been overestimated.

label: text
text: While it is out of the scope of this report to try to analyse and find the true cause of the pre-RTB reforms downtrend in the proportion of broader patents, it would still be useful to try to get a sense of the magnitude. To do this, we re-estimate the regression model using 2012 as the "treatment"

label: text
text: year. We also restrict the window of analysis to be as narrow as possible, and to start from 2011 and end at 30 June 2013. The idea is that in theory in this window there is no effect from RTB reforms except for the "anticipatory" or the unknown effect.

label: text
text: The result of the regression estimates is summarised in Table 10. As shown in Column (3), the magnitude of the unknown or anticipatory effect is -0.016. Compared to the baseline estimates shown in Table 2 (Column 6) which is reproduced in Table 10's columns 1, the true RTB effect could be as high as 5.8 percentage points reduction in the proportion of broader patents (if the -1.6 percentage points downtrend is caused by anticipatory factors related to RTB) or as low as -2.7 percentage points (if the -1.6 percentage points downtrend is caused by factors unrelated to RTB).

This suggests that the reforms have likely impacted patent scope across the entire distribution, not just the patents that would otherwise have been broader in scope.

However, the same figure also shows a decrease in the proportion of similar patent scope classification manually assessed, but the corresponding coefficient estimate on column (1) of Table 12 is not statistically significant. Furthermore, on further analysis based on separate AU-EP and AU-US sample not reported in Table 12, we find that the negative impact estimate of RTB is not statistically significant for the AU-EP sample.
